title: Surviving the Overfitting Gauntlet, Part II: NIFTY on the 15-Minute
author: Nhuga_Official
selftext:
https://i.redd.it/ebe1e2cso0xh1.png

*Eleven signals cleared every gate. Here's the standard they had to meet — and why, in my view, almost nothing you see posted would.*

# Eleven survived

I ran a family of NIFTY 15-minute strategies through a four-gate statistical gauntlet built to catch luck wearing a lab coat. **Eleven cleared it.** Last time, the same machine killed 18 of 20 gold strategies and let 2 through.

That's the headline. The rest of this is *why* clearing it means something — because, I'll say up front as a view and not a law: most strategies that *look* profitable are telling you a story, not showing you evidence.

A high win rate, on its own, is not evidence. A clean equity curve is not evidence. A short run of winning trades is not evidence — a lucky streak looks identical to skill from the inside, and when many strategies are being tried at once, someone's streak is always still running. The person holding it feels like a genius. The maths just shrugs.

What I'd accept as evidence is narrower: **a result too good, too consistent, across too many independent conditions to be comfortably explained by luck.** So the question I care about isn't "did it make money in the backtest?" Almost anything can. It's: *how hard did you try to prove it was an accident — and did it survive?*

# The gauntlet

Before I'll treat a signal as an edge, it has to walk through four doors. Each one is built to kill it, and in my runs most candidates die at the first.

**1. Plateau robustness.** A real edge, in my view, shouldn't live on one magic setting. If a strategy works beautifully but falls apart the moment you nudge a single parameter by one notch, I read that as a coincidence balanced on a spike. So I sweep the whole neighbourhood of parameters, require the strategy to stay positive across *all* of it, and quote the result from the *middle* of that plateau — never the peak, because peaks are where overfitting tends to hide.

**2. Walk-forward.** Fit on the past, score on a future the fit never saw, rolling forward through time. The in-sample number barely matters to me. What matters is that the **sign holds out-of-sample**: something positive when it was discovered stays positive on data it was never shown.

**3. PBO — Probability of Backtest Overfitting.** Try enough configurations and one will top the leaderboard by chance alone. PBO estimates the odds the "best" strategy is best by luck. My gate: **≤ 0.40.**

**4. DSR — Deflated Sharpe Ratio.** A Sharpe of 1.0 means one thing if you tested a single idea and something very different if you tested five hundred. DSR deflates the headline Sharpe for how many trials it took, plus skew and fat tails, then reports the probability the true edge is above zero. My gate: **≥ 0.95.**

Pass one door and you have a backtest. Pass all four and — the way I'd put it — the strategy has earned a *provisional* right to be believed: the way a scientist trusts a result that hasn't yet been falsified.

# What survived on NIFTY

After the gauntlet, **eleven signals were left standing** on NIFTY 15-minute — trend-following, breakout, and volume-flow families, all long-only, holding overnight. The specific recipes stay in-house; what's worth sharing is the shape of what survives.

|Signal (family)|Net Sharpe|PBO (≤0.40)|DSR (≥0.95)|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Trend-following · A|**1.22**|0.11|0.998|
|Trend-following · B|1.09|0.16|0.995|
|Trend-following · C|1.08|**0.01**|0.980|
|Trend-following · D|1.08|0.33|0.966|
|Trend-following · E|1.05|0.09|0.989|
|Breakout · A|1.00|0.34|0.981|
|Trend-following · F|0.93|0.14|0.976|
|Trend-following · G|0.93|0.36|0.969|
|Flow · A|0.86|0.16|0.972|
|Flow · B|0.83|0.16|0.985|
|Flow · C|0.73|0.16|0.969|

*One note on that 0.01: PBO measures how stable a configuration's ranking is within the grid it was tested on — so a very low value on a tightly-correlated long-trend grid, where neighbouring settings are almost the same strategy, is expected rather than extraordinary.*

# The receipt, for the strongest one

Take **Trend-following · A**, the top of the table. Here's its full card, not a highlight:

* **Plateau:** chosen from a **20-setting parameter grid where all 20 came out positive** — not one magic cell. I took the plateau-median region (Sharpe **1.22**), not the peak of **1.36**.
* **Walk-forward:** four rolling out-of-sample windows, **all four positive** (0.19, 1.75, 1.95, 0.91), path Sharpe **1.28**, sign held. In-sample was 1.40, out-of-sample settled lower — which is exactly the honest direction for it to move.
* **Gates:** PBO **0.11**, DSR **0.998**.

That's deliberately *less* exciting than a peak-fitted curve. That's the point.

Two honesty notes, because a result you can't poke at isn't worth much:

* These are the **signal edges** — the discovery leg, traded naked: no stop-loss overlay, no volatility targeting. Net Sharpe is that discovery-leg figure; the exit and sizing layer is a separate study.
* What this summary *doesn't* show — trade count, max drawdown, exact test span — lives in the full run log, not the survivor card. I'd rather hand you the gate statistics than a cherry-picked equity screenshot. And clearing the gauntlet is, to me, a licence to **forward-test with small size** — not to bet the account. It lowers the odds I'm fooling myself. It doesn't abolish them.

# The part nobody checks: the candles themselves

Here's a failure mode that, in my experience, quietly breaks more backtests than overfitting ever does — **the data underneath the strategy is wrong, and nobody looked.**

Every one of these signals trades the 15-minute bar. So before trusting a single result, I rebuilt NIFTY's candles from raw 5-minute data and checked them, bar for bar, against TradingView — the chart most people actually trade off.

* **Across the span I checked — 15-minute, 30-minute, 1-hour, 2-hour, 4-hour — they matched exactly.** Open, high, low, close *and* volume, every bar, zero difference.
* **The daily bar is the one I'd warn against rebuilding from intraday.** A resampled day can't recover the pre-open print or the closing auction, so its open, close and volume drift from the official daily — by a little most days, and on one settlement day in my sample by roughly half the volume. Daily should come from a native daily feed.

That second point isn't a bug — I'd call it the discipline. An edge is only as real as the candles it's measured on, and that's a check I'd argue gets skipped far more often than it should.

# How to tell a real edge from a lucky one

You don't need my machine for the lesson. The next time a strategy crosses your feed, these are the questions I'd ask:

1. **How many trades?** As a rough rule, under \~30 the win rate is mostly noise. A handful is close to a coin flip with a caption.
2. **One regime, or many?** A few calm months is one draw, not several independent tests. Did it ever face a crash, a gap, a trend day?
3. **In-sample or out-of-sample?** If the only data it's seen is the data it was tuned on, you've been shown a memory, not a prediction.
4. **How many things were tried before this one won?** The more configurations tested, the higher the Sharpe needs to be to mean anything.
5. **Does the data even match the chart?** The most basic question — and, in my experience, the one asked least.

A strategy that can answer all five is rare. That rarity, I'd argue, is the whole point: the market tends to pay for edges precisely because most of what looks like one is a coin that hasn't landed tails yet.

# What happens next

Eleven signals cleared the gauntlet on NIFTY this week. Over the coming weeks I'll post the forward test **here, in the open** — the same eleven, live, no edits, whether they hold up or break. Follow along if you want to watch that happen in public rather than take my word for it.

*Not investment advice — this is a research log, not a recommendation to trade anything.*

*— Nhuga. We don't post the wins. We post the gauntlet.*

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good write-up, and it's useful to see the gate numbers instead of a single equity curve. One thing I'd check is that the 11 survivors come from the same long-only grid on one index, so they're probably close to one bet, and the DSR trial count should include every setting you tried across all families. Because NIFTY was in a long uptrend over most of the period, a long-only overnight rule could pass every gate just on drift, so I'd compare it against a random long-only strategy with the same time in the market. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to run that kind of baseline check.
